extraction.name: CADS: A Comprehensive Anatomical Dataset and Segmentation for Whole-Body Anatomy in Computed Tomography
extraction.description: CADS is an open-source framework designed to address the fragmented landscape of AI-based whole-body CT segmentation by systematically integrating, standardizing, and labeling heterogeneous cross-institutional and cross-vendor data sources. The framework comprises two main components: CADS-dataset and CADS-model. CADS-dataset is a large-scale collection of 22,022 CT volumes with complete annotations for 167 anatomical structures, representing a significant advancement in both scale and coverage. CADS-model is a robust, fully automated segmentation model suite trained on the CADS-dataset, capable of segmenting 167 structures from head to knee across diverse anatomical systems. The framework is validated through comprehensive evaluation across 18 public datasets and an independent real-world hospital cohort, demonstrating advantages over state-of-the-art approaches.

extraction.rai:dataCollection: The CADS-dataset aggregates 22,022 CT volumes from 40 diverse sources, including public archives (e.g., TCIA, medical challenges), hospital cohorts, and newly contributed images. The collection spans over 100 imaging facilities across 16 countries, capturing varied clinical practices and patient populations. Geographic diversity includes data from Austria, Belgium, Canada, Switzerland, China, Germany, Spain, France, Israel, Italy, Japan, Netherlands, Portugal, Slovenia, Turkey, and the United States. The dataset includes varying imaging protocols (contrast-enhanced and non-contrast acquisitions) and covers multiple anatomical regions through different fields of view: whole-body, head-and-neck, chest, abdomen, pelvis, and spine. The data collection strategy systematically consolidates CT scans and annotations from three main sources: (1) large-scale public archives including TotalSegmentator (1,203 annotated volumes with comprehensive coverage of 104 anatomical structures), the National Lung Screening Trial (NLST, 7,172 scans), CT-RATE (3,134 scans), and AbdomenCT-1K (1,062 scans); (2) specialized annotation collections from medical imaging challenges (via Grand Challenge and MICCAI) and focused research studies; and (3) newly contributed images and annotations, comprising manual annotations of critical OARs on the VISCERAL dataset, 484 newly acquired anonymized head CTs, and 586 triphasic contrast-enhanced abdominal CT scans.

extraction.rai:dataCollectionMissingData: The dataset includes 21% of volumes with partial annotations from public sources, while 79% lack any annotations. Missingness is explicitly discussed in the context of the annotation pipeline, where pseudo-labeling is used to address the imbalance between labeled and unlabeled data.
extraction.rai:dataCollectionRawData: The raw data sources include public archives (e.g., TCIA, medical challenges), hospital cohorts, and newly contributed images. Specific datasets include TotalSegmentator, National Lung Screening Trial (NLST), CT-RATE, AbdomenCT-1K, VISCERAL Gold Corpus, VISCERAL Silver Corpus, KiTS, LiTS, BTCV-Abdomen, BTCV-Cervix, CHAOS, VerSe, EXACT09, CAD-PE, RibFrac, Leam2reg, LNDb, LOLA11, SLIVER07, STOIC2021, EMPIRE10, AMOS, HaN-Seg, CT-ORG, LIDC-IDRI, CT Lymph Nodes, CPTAC-CCRCC, CPTAC-LUAD, CT Images in COVID-19, NSCLC Radiogenomics, Pancreas-CT, Pancreatic-CT-CBCTSEG, RIDER Lung CT, TCGA-KICH, TCGA-KIRC, TCGA-KIRP, TCGA-LIHC, and newly acquired head and abdominal CT scans from clinical collaborators.
extraction.rai:dataManipulationProtocol: The dataset underwent preprocessing and standardization, including reorientation to RAS convention, resampling to 1.5 mm isotropic resolution, and simplification of affine transformation matrices. Facial features in newly acquired head CT scans were anonymized using a Gaussian filter (σ=5 voxels at 1.5 mm spacing).
extraction.rai:dataPreprocessingProtocol: The preprocessing pipeline includes: (1) reorientation to RAS convention; (2) resampling to 1.5 mm isotropic resolution; (3) simplification of affine transformation matrices by removing rotation and translation components; (4) anonymization of facial features in newly acquired head CT scans using a Gaussian filter (σ=5 voxels at 1.5 mm spacing).
extraction.rai:dataAnnotationProtocol: The annotation process involved: (1) organizing 167 target structures into nine anatomical groups and developing specialized models for each group; (2) using high-quality annotations from established datasets (e.g., TotalSegmentator, VISCERAL Gold Corpus) as a foundation; (3) employing self-training through iterative model refinement, shape-guided quality control of segmentations, and fusion of the best-performing annotations from multiple segmentation approaches; (4) implementing structure-specific quality controls and refinements, such as rib segmentation correction to preserve costovertebral joints; (5) using a multi-stage annotation process involving pseudo-labeling, shape-informed label quality control, and multi-strategy label generation through an ensemble selection mechanism.
extraction.rai:dataAnnotationPlatform: nnU-Net framework, 3D Slicer, vesselFM, ANTS non-rigid transformation, SimNIBS MRI atlas
extraction.rai:dataAnnotationAnalysis: The annotation analysis involved: (1) statistical ranking and selection of model flavors (GT, Pseudo, Shape) based on performance metrics (Dice, HD95) on in-distribution and out-of-distribution validation data; (2) evaluating segmentation quality using Dice Similarity Coefficient (Dice) as the primary metric and 95-percentile Hausdorff distance (HD95) as a secondary metric; (3) performing normality and variance equality tests (Shapiro-Wilk, Levene) to select appropriate statistical tests (ANOVA, Welch’s ANOVA, Kruskal-Wallis) and post-hoc comparisons (Tukey’s HSD, Dunn’s test); (4) identifying significant differences (p < 0.05) between flavors to determine the most reliable segmentation for each anatomical structure.
extraction.rai:annotationsPerItem: The number of human labels per dataset item varies by structure and dataset. For example, the VISCERAL Gold Corpus dataset has 40 volumes with 20 annotated structures, while the TotalSegmentator dataset has 1,203 volumes with 104 annotated structures. The annotation process also involves multi-strategy label generation, where three model flavors (GT, Pseudo, Shape) are evaluated and combined to create final labels.
extraction.rai:annotatorDemographics: The annotators include medical research assistants, a radiation oncologist, and domain experts. The team comprises individuals from multiple institutions, including the University of Zurich, ETH Zurich, University Hospital Zurich, Istanbul Medipol University, Technical University of Munich, and others. The annotators contributed to manual annotations of critical OARs on the VISCERAL dataset, as well as newly acquired head and abdominal CT scans.
extraction.rai:machineAnnotationTools: nnU-Net, vesselFM, ANTS non-rigid transformation, SimNIBS MRI atlas, neural implicit functions, shape priors
extraction.rai:dataReleaseMaintenancePlan: The CADS framework is released as an open-source framework with versioning information, maintainers, and deprecation policies. The dataset, models, and tools are publicly available via Hugging Face (https://huggingface.co/datasets/mrmrx/CADS-dataset) and GitHub (https://github.com/murong-xu/CADS, https://github.com/murong-xu/SlicerCADS). The framework includes a 3D Slicer plugin for accessible deployment. The release includes comprehensive documentation and user instructions for reproducibility and adoption.
extraction.rai:personalSensitiveInformation: The dataset includes facial features in newly acquired head CT scans, which are anonymized using a Gaussian filter (σ=5 voxels at 1.5 mm spacing) to obscure identity while preserving anatomical integrity. The dataset also includes patient demographics and pathological conditions, such as oncological diseases (carcinomas, lymphomas, metastases), COVID-19, traumatic injuries, and rare disorders.
extraction.rai:dataSocialImpact: The CADS framework aims to advance robust AI solutions in radiology and make comprehensive anatomical analysis accessible to clinicians and researchers. The framework enables various research directions beyond segmentation, including anatomical landmark detection, cross-modality registration, anatomy-guided synthesis, longitudinal organ tracking, personalized anatomical modeling, radiation treatment planning, and large-scale population studies. The clinical potential spans multiple domains: in radiation oncology, it can streamline treatment planning through rapid organ delineation; in diagnostic radiology, it can enable automated organ volume quantification and detection of subtle anatomical changes; and for research applications, it can facilitate large-scale studies across diverse populations and conditions.
extraction.rai:dataBiases: The dataset includes biases related to imaging protocols, patient populations, and institutional practices. The collection spans over 100 imaging facilities across 16 countries, capturing varied clinical practices and patient populations. The dataset includes varying imaging protocols (contrast-enhanced and non-contrast acquisitions) and covers multiple anatomical regions. The annotation process also introduces biases, such as systematic errors in complex anatomical structures like ribs and vertebrae, which are addressed through structure-specific quality controls and refinements.
extraction.rai:dataLimitations: Known limitations include: (1) exclusion of atypical anatomical variations (e.g., lumbar sacralization, thoracic lumbarization) in evaluation datasets; (2) intentional anonymization of facial features in newly acquired head CT scans, limiting applications requiring detailed facial analysis; (3) challenges in segmenting very small organs (e.g., arytenoid cartilage) and anatomically complex structures (e.g., small glands) due to limited training data and standard CT resolution limits; (4) potential limitations in generalizing to regions outside the head-to-knee coverage; (5) reliance on pseudo-labeling for unlabeled data, which may introduce noise and inaccuracies; (6) exclusion of cases with pathological conditions presenting atypical anatomical variations in the shape-based quality assessment process.
extraction.rai:dataUseCases: The dataset is designed for training, testing, validation, and fine-tuning of AI models for whole-body CT segmentation. Use cases include: (1) development of robust, clinically viable segmentation models; (2) anatomical landmark detection; (3) cross-modality registration; (4) anatomy-guided synthesis; (5) longitudinal organ tracking; (6) personalized anatomical modeling; (7) radiation treatment planning; (8) large-scale population studies. The framework is validated for clinical utility in radiation oncology, demonstrating direct utility for precision therapeutic planning. The dataset is also suitable for research applications in diagnostic radiology and medical imaging analysis.
